x.ASV: Praise ye Jehovah. Blessed is the man that feareth Jehovah, That delighteth greatly in his commandments.
x.Darby: Hallelujah! Blessed is the man that feareth Jehovah, that delighteth greatly in his commandments.
x.KJV: Praise ye the Lord. Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord, that delighteth greatly in his commandments.
x.YLT: Praise ye Jah! O the happiness of one fearing Jehovah, In His commands he hath delighted greatly.

nt: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is] or [Truly blessed is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means any man who fears Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [how happy is the one who greatly delights in his commandments]

x.ASV: His seed shall be mighty upon earth: The generation of the upright shall be blessed.
x.Darby: His seed shall be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright shall be blessed.
x.KJV: His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed.
x.YLT: Mighty in the earth is his seed, The generation of the upright is blessed.

nt: Here the psalmist is speaking of the man’s children as if they were **seed** that he had planted. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [His offspring]

The expression **will be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will bless a generation of upright ones]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **a generation** that is characterized by being **upright**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [everyone who is upright]

x.ASV: Wealth and riches are in his house; And his righteousness endureth for ever.
x.Darby: Wealth and riches [shall be] in his house; and his righteousness abideth for ever.
x.KJV: Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever.
x.YLT: Wealth and riches are in his house, And his righteousness is standing for ever.

nt: The terms **Wealth** and **riches** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Abundant riches]

The psalmist is using the term **house** to mean an entire household living together. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [belong to his household]
The pronoun **his** refers to the man who fears Yahweh mentioned in verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [belong to such a person]
The pronoun **his** refers to the man who fears Yahweh from verse 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the righteousness of such a person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and each righteous thing that he does]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh and/or people will always remember the righteous things that such a person does. Alternate translation: [continues to be remembered forever] or (2) Such people never stop doing righteous deeds. Alternate translation: [keeps going continually]

x.ASV: Unto the upright there ariseth light in the darkness: He is gracious, and merciful, and righteous.
x.Darby: Unto the upright there ariseth light in the darkness; he is gracious, and merciful, and righteous.
x.KJV: Unto the upright there ariseth light in the darkness: he is gracious, and full of compassion, and righteous.
x.YLT: Light hath risen in darkness to the upright, Gracious, and merciful, and righteous.

nt: Here, **Light** could be: (1) the subject of the verb **shines** as in the ULT, or (2) the object of the verb **shines**, and then the subject of the verb would be “he,” continuing the subject of the previous verse. Alternate translation: [He shines light in the darkness for the upright]

The psalmist speaks of God blessing the upright person in difficult times as if his blessings were a **light** shining in darkness. Alternate translation: [The blessings that an upright person receives from God are like a light that shines in the darkness]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [such a person is gracious and compassionate and just]

x.ASV: Well is it with the man that dealeth graciously and lendeth; He shall maintain his cause in judgment.
x.Darby: It is well with the man that is gracious and lendeth; he will sustain his cause in judgment.
x.KJV: A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion.
x.YLT: Good is the man--gracious and lending, He sustaineth his matters in judgment.

nt: This could mean: (1) it is good to be person who is gracious and lends freely. Alternate translation: [It is good to be a gracious and lending man] or (2) good things will happen to a man who is gracious and lending. Alternate translation: [Life goes well for a gracious and lending man]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a gracious and lending person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is just in all his dealings]

x.ASV: For he shall never be moved; The righteous shall be had in everlasting remembrance.
x.Darby: For he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.
x.KJV: Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.
x.YLT: For--to the age he is not moved; For a memorial age-during is the righteous.

nt: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [He does this because he will not be moved for forever]

The expression **he will not be moved** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For nothing will move him for forever]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the righteous person as if he were an object that could be **moved** from its place. He means that nothing will cause the righteous person to fail or be overcome by difficulties. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [For nothing will ever cause him to fail]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will always be remembered]

x.ASV: He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: His heart is fixed, trusting in Jehovah.
x.Darby: He shall not be afraid of evil tidings; his heart is fixed confiding in Jehovah;
x.KJV: He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the Lord.
x.YLT: Of an evil report he is not afraid, Prepared is His heart, confident in Jehovah.

nt: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The psalmist is speaking of a person’s inner confidence as if it were **sure**, meaning firmly established or steadfast. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is confident]

x.ASV: His heart is established, he shall not be afraid, Until he see his desire upon his adversaries.
x.Darby: His heart is maintained, he is not afraid, until he see [his desire] upon his oppressors.
x.KJV: His heart is established, he shall not be afraid, until he see his desire upon his enemies.
x.YLT: Sustained is his heart--he feareth not, Till that he look on his adversaries.

nt: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. The psalmist is speaking of the righteous person’s emotional state as if his **heart** were **upheld** or supported, meaning that he is calm. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He is tranquil]

The implication is that the righteous person will remain confident and unafraid while God vindicates him by defeating his enemies. This does not mean that he will begin to fear when he sees his enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all the way to the time that he looks triumphantly over his adversaries]

x.ASV: He hath dispersed, he hath given to the needy; His righteousness endureth for ever: His horn shall be exalted with honor.
x.Darby: He scattereth abroad, he giveth to the needy; his righteousness abideth for ever: his horn shall be exalted with honour.
x.KJV: He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honour.
x.YLT: He hath scattered--hath given to the needy, His righteousness is standing for ever, His horn is exalted with honour.

nt: The terms **scatters** and **gives** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He gives generously]

The psalmist is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to anyone who is poor]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his righteous works stand forever]

This could mean: (1) Yahweh and/or people will always remember the righteous things that such a person does. Alternate translation: [his righteousness continues to be remembered forever] or (2) Such people never stop doing righteous deeds. Alternate translation: [his righteousness keeps going continually]

The psalmist is using **his horn is high** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he is honored and respected by others.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people respect and honor him]

x.ASV: The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; He shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: The desire of the wicked shall perish.
x.Darby: The wicked [man] shall see [it] and be vexed; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish.
x.KJV: The wicked shall see it, and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish.
x.YLT: The wicked seeth, and hath been angry, His teeth he gnasheth, and hath melted, The desire of the wicked doth perish!

nt: The implication is that the wicked will see the prosperity and honor of the righteous person described in the previous verses. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The wicked will see these things happen]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Wicked people will see]
The grinding of teeth is an expression of extreme anger. See how you translated a similar phrase in [Psalms 35:16](../035/016.md). Alternate translation: [he will grind his teeth in rage]

Here the psalmist is speaking of the wicked person as if he were something that could **melt away** like ice or wax. He means that the wicked person will become unimportant and die. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will become unimportant and die]

Here, **desire** could mean: (1) the emotional desire that wicked people have to do wicked things. Alternate translation: [the things that wicked people want to do will never happen] or (2) it represents the things that wicked people have desired. Alternate translation: [wicked people will lose the things that they desired to have]
